title: NURS 1017 Unit 7 Case Study 8

question.stem: The nurse reviews the client's history and assessment. Which findings require follow-up? Select all that apply.

options.text: Temperature 36.9° C
Numbness of the fingertips, unchanged for 2 years
Needs help to walk to the bathroom because of weak, stiff legs and an unsteady gait
Weakness is much worse after a hot shower
Wears glasses for reading
Bladder scan of 350 mL after voiding
Limits her fluid intake to about 800 mL a day
Double vision when looking to the left
States she has stopped seeing friends and feels like a burden

question.explanation:
Require follow-up: new leg weakness, stiffness (spasticity), an unsteady gait and double vision put her at high risk of falling. A post-void residual of 350 mL means her bladder is not emptying (urinary retention), and limiting fluids to avoid accidents concentrates the urine; both raise the risk of a urinary tract infection. Withdrawing from friends and feeling like a burden can signal depression, which is common in MS and needs screening and support. Worsening weakness after a hot shower (heat sensitivity) is important for safety and teaching.

Do not require follow-up now: fingertip numbness that has not changed in 2 years is her baseline (the nurse documents it to compare with later). A normal temperature is expected (and reassuring, because infection and fever can worsen MS symptoms). Reading glasses are unrelated.

Why MS causes these findings: MS is an autoimmune disease in which immune cells attack the myelin of the brain, optic nerves and spinal cord. Inflamed, demyelinated areas (plaques) slow or block nerve conduction, so symptoms depend on where the plaques are: motor weakness and spasticity, double vision, bladder dysfunction, sensory changes and fatigue. In a relapse, new inflammation causes new or worse symptoms over days; they often improve as inflammation settles (remission).

leftContent.intro: The nurse on a medical unit is caring for a 34-year-old female client with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (MS).

question.stem: For each finding, click to specify the nursing problem or problems it contributes to: risk for falls, risk for urinary tract infection, or fatigue. Each finding may contribute to more than one problem.

rows.text: Weak, stiff legs with an unsteady gait
Gets up to void 4 times a night
Drinks only about 800 mL a day
Weakness worse after a hot shower

question.explanation:
Risk for falls: weakness, spasticity and poor balance, double vision (impaired depth perception), hurried trips to the bathroom at night in the dark, and the temporary weakness that follows heat exposure.

Risk for urinary tract infection: urine left in the bladder (retention) lets bacteria multiply, and a low fluid intake reduces flushing of the urinary tract. A urinary tract infection, or any fever, can temporarily worsen MS symptoms (a pseudo-relapse), so prevention matters.

Fatigue: the most common MS symptom; demyelinated nerves need more energy to conduct impulses. Broken sleep from nocturia and heat make it worse. Heat slows conduction in demyelinated nerves even more, so symptoms worsen temporarily after a hot shower, exercise in the heat, or a fever (and improve with cooling).

cloze.text: The nurse's priority problem for the client is [[drop0]] because of [[drop1]]. The nurse also addresses her [[drop2]], which increases her risk of [[drop3]].

question.explanation:
Risk for falls is the priority: it is an immediate safety threat. A fall could cause a fracture or head injury and set back her recovery and independence. Her weakness, gait, double vision and nocturia together make a fall likely, especially at night.

Urinary retention and low fluid intake come next: they raise the risk of a urinary tract infection, which can worsen MS symptoms and, if untreated, damage the kidneys. Fatigue and mood are also addressed in the plan, but they are not as urgent as her physical safety.

leftContent.intro: The nurse on a medical unit is caring for a 34-year-old female client with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (MS).

question.stem: Which interventions should the nurse include in the client's plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Plan care and activities with rest periods in between
Ask open-ended questions about her mood and coping, and involve her husband if she wishes
Apply a heating pad to her stiff legs
Encourage her to stay in bed until the relapse resolves
Insert an indwelling urinary catheter to keep her bladder empty
Keep the bed in the lowest position with the call bell and a urinal or commode within reach at night
Offer lukewarm, not hot, showers with a shower chair
Encourage a fluid intake of about 2 L a day, spread over the day and reduced in the evening

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Provider Orders.
question.explanation:
Include: a low bed, the call bell and a commode or urinal close by reduce night-time falls. Pacing activities with rest conserves energy. A fluid intake of about 2 L a day prevents urinary tract infections; reducing fluids in the evening lessens nocturia. Lukewarm water and a shower chair avoid heat-related weakness and falls. Talking openly about mood, coping and family roles, with the social worker's help, supports her mental health. Physiotherapy (strength, stretching for spasticity, balance, a walking aid) and occupational therapy (energy conservation, home and work adaptations) are part of the team plan.

Do not include: bed rest causes deconditioning and contractures; she stays as active as she safely can. A heating pad can worsen symptoms and can burn skin with reduced sensation. An indwelling catheter greatly raises infection risk; intermittent catheterization (done by the nurse, then by the client) empties the bladder with less risk and supports independence.

leftContent.intro: The nurse on a medical unit is caring for a 34-year-old female client with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (MS).

question.stem: Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Stay with her and listen to her concerns
Hold the next methylprednisolone dose until the provider sees her in the morning
Report the glucose, BP, insomnia and mood changes to the provider
Encourage her to walk the hallway alone until she feels tired
Ask her directly whether she is having thoughts of harming herself or ending her life
Tell her that steroids always cause these feelings, so she should try to ignore them
Help her back to bed and offer measures that promote sleep, such as dimming the lights and limiting interruptions

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 3 0200, the Vital Signs from Day 3 0200 and the Laboratory Results.
question.explanation:
Correct: a statement of hopelessness is followed by a direct question about suicidal thoughts; asking does not put the idea in the person's mind, and it guides immediate safety measures (in Canada, the 9-8-8 Suicide Crisis Helpline is also available). Staying with her and listening shows respect and lets her express her fears. High-dose corticosteroids commonly cause insomnia, mood changes, hyperglycemia and raised BP; these are reported so the provider can treat them (for example, insulin for glucose, a sleep aid, giving the dose early in the day). Sleep-promoting measures help.

Incorrect: dismissing her feelings blocks communication and may miss depression or suicide risk. The nurse does not hold a prescribed dose without consulting the provider. Walking alone at night with weak legs and double vision risks a fall.

leftContent.intro: The nurse on a medical unit is caring for a 34-year-old female client with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (MS).

question.stem: For each statement, click to specify whether it indicates an understanding of the discharge teaching or a need for further teaching.

rows.text: Client: “I'll wash my hands and the catheter, and catheterize every 6 hours, even when I'm busy at work.”
Husband: “She should stop the disease-modifying injections once she feels back to normal.”
Client: “If my urine burns, smells bad, or I get a fever, I'll call the MS clinic.”
Client: “I'll use my walker at home until physiotherapy says I can stop.”
Client: “I'll save my errands for the hottest part of the afternoon, when I've had time to rest.”
Husband: “We'll ask the occupational therapist about setting up the kitchen so she can sit while she works.”
Client: “I'll keep my counselling appointments, even if I'm feeling better.”

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from Day 7 1000.
question.explanation:
Understanding: clean technique and a regular schedule for self-catheterization prevent infection and overdistension. Signs of a urinary tract infection are reported early, because infection can worsen MS symptoms. Using the walker until physiotherapy advises otherwise prevents falls. Sitting to work and arranging the kitchen are energy-conservation strategies. Continuing counselling supports her coping over the long term.

Needs further teaching: disease-modifying therapies reduce relapses and slow disability; they are continued between relapses, when she feels well, and are changed only with the neurologist. Heat worsens MS symptoms, so errands are planned for the cooler parts of the day, with cooling strategies (air conditioning, cooling vest, cool drinks).

description: 34-year-old female client with a relapse of multiple sclerosis: focused neurological assessment, falls, urinary retention and infection risk, fatigue and heat sensitivity, nursing priorities and an interprofessional plan, mood and safety during high-dose corticosteroids, and discharge teaching for self-catheterization, energy conservation and ongoing therapy.

New case written by Claude on 2 Nov 2026 for the Unit 7 learning outcomes; please review before using it with students:
